title: China: the price-setter next door
hook:
In May 2025, on what should have been a routine earnings call, an executive at Bajaj Auto said something that made the whole Indian auto industry sit up. There was, he warned, a dark cloud over the supply of magnets from China. Not engines, not chips. Magnets: small blocks of rare-earth metal that sit inside every electric motor. China had started demanding export licences and paperwork for them, shipments were stuck at Chinese ports, and if nothing moved, production would start to suffer within weeks. Maruti Suzuki quietly cut its early production targets for its first electric car.

Now hold that picture next to another one from the same year. India was assembling a large and fast-growing share of the world's iPhones, much of it shipped straight to America, because Chinese-made phones faced far steeper US tariffs. Factories in Tamil Nadu and Karnataka were winning business that, a decade earlier, would have gone to Shenzhen without a second thought.

That is China for an Indian investor in one year: the competitor whose prices you cannot beat, the supplier you cannot do without, and the rival whose troubles hand you orders. This chapter untangles those three roles, explains how each one reaches Indian stock prices, and tells you what to watch.
short: China builds more than it buys. Since its property bust, the surplus of steel, chemicals, solar gear and cars has been exported cheaply, which caps what Indian producers can charge.

For Indian metals and chemicals, the Chinese export price is effectively the ceiling. Anti-dumping and safeguard duties are the cushion, and they help producers at the expense of the industries that buy from them.
China plus one brings real orders to India, but much of the value still sits in Chinese components. Assembly is moving faster than the supply chain behind it.
Rare earths showed that dependence is a lever China is willing to pull. The October 2025 expansion of controls was paused for a year, not withdrawn.
Copper against gold is a decent live read of Chinese and global factory demand, and Indian metal stocks tend to follow it.

sections.heading: Why China keeps making more than it can use
sections.html:
Start with the engine. For two decades China grew by building: apartments, roads, railways, ports, factories. Property alone became the biggest store of household wealth in the country, and the steel, cement, copper and glass that went into it made China the largest buyer of almost every industrial commodity on earth.

Then, in August 2020, Beijing decided the developers had borrowed too much. It set three red lines: limits on debt against assets, debt against equity, and cash against short-term borrowing. Breach them and you could not take new bank loans. Evergrande, the most indebted developer in the world, breached all three. It started missing payments in 2021, and the rest of the sector followed it down. Home sales slumped, prices fell, and Chinese families who had parked their savings in apartments felt poorer and spent less.

Here's the thing. A normal economy facing a slump in demand would close some factories. China did the opposite. State banks steered credit away from property and towards manufacturing, especially the industries Beijing wants to dominate: electric vehicles, batteries, solar panels, chips, advanced materials. Factories kept running. Capacity kept rising. But the people who were supposed to buy all that output were cutting back.

When a country makes far more than it consumes, the surplus has to go somewhere, and it goes abroad at whatever price clears it. That shows up in one statistic economists watch closely: producer prices, the prices factories charge at the gate before any retail markup. China's producer prices have spent long stretches falling since the property bust. Falling factory-gate prices at home mean Chinese exporters can cut prices abroad and still keep the lines running.

China's deflation does not stay in China. It gets packed into containers and shipped to everyone else.

China does not have to target India for its surplus to land here. India is simply a large, growing market with tariffs low enough, in many products, to make it worth the trip.

sections.heading: How a Chinese price becomes an Indian ceiling
sections.html:
Think about how an Indian steelmaker sets its price. It is not cost plus margin. A big buyer, say a carmaker or a pipe manufacturer, can always ask: what would it cost me to import this instead? That number is called import parity: the overseas price, plus freight, plus insurance, plus any customs duty, plus the hassle of waiting for a ship. Domestic mills can charge up to roughly that level and not much more, because above it buyers simply import.

So when Chinese mills, stuck with steel nobody at home wants, cut their export offers, the import parity price in India drops too, and Indian mills have to follow even if their own costs have not changed. Their margins get squeezed from the top. The marginal tonne sets the price for everyone.

The same logic runs through a long list of products. Chemicals are the classic case. Indian specialty chemical makers enjoyed a boom around 2020 and 2021, when Chinese plants were shut for pollution checks and lockdowns and global buyers wanted a second source. When Chinese capacity came roaring back and its own demand stayed weak, prices for many intermediates and agrochemicals sank, and several Indian chemical stocks that had been priced for endless growth gave back much of their gains. Solar modules, glass, aluminium products, tyres, ceramics, and increasingly cars and electronics follow the same pattern.

There is a flip side, and it matters. Cheap Chinese inputs are a gift to whoever buys them. An Indian company assembling solar farms, making appliances, or building infrastructure pays less when Chinese prices fall. Consumers get cheaper goods. That is why the government has to keep choosing, product by product, whether to protect the makers or the users. Which brings us to the shock absorber.

sections.heading: Anti-dumping duties: India's shock absorber, and who pays for it
sections.html:
Dumping, in trade law, means selling abroad below what you charge at home, or below cost. When an Indian industry thinks that is happening, it files a complaint with the Directorate General of Trade Remedies, a small office inside the commerce ministry that has become one of the busiest trade-defence agencies in the world.

The agency investigates whether the imports are priced below normal value, whether Indian producers have actually been hurt, and whether one caused the other. If it finds all three, it recommends a duty sized to close the gap, and the finance ministry decides whether to impose it. Duties usually run for years, not months. A large share of India's cases involve Chinese goods,.

When the threat is a flood rather than a single unfair seller, India can use a broader tool: a safeguard duty, which applies to imports from many countries at once. In April 2025, after complaints from the big steelmakers, India imposed a temporary safeguard duty on flat steel imports. Look at how it was designed. The duty did not apply above certain floor prices. In other words, it was aimed squarely at the cheapest steel coming in, which mostly meant China and Vietnam, while leaving expensive specialty grades alone.

Now the part that is easy to miss. Every duty that helps a producer hurts a user. A safeguard on steel lifts the margins of steel mills, and raises costs for the thousands of small engineering firms, auto component makers and fabricators that buy steel. A duty on a chemical intermediate helps the company making it and squeezes the companies that turn it into paint, plastics or medicines.

So when a new duty is announced, the professional question is not whether it is good for India. It is which side of the trade a company sits on, and how much of the protection it can actually keep before prices adjust.

sections.heading: Reading China's pulse from a single chart
sections.html:
China publishes plenty of statistics, but markets have long preferred a few prices that are harder to dress up. One of the best is the ratio of copper to gold.

The logic is simple. Copper goes into wiring, motors, buildings, power grids and cars, and China is by far its biggest buyer. When Chinese factories and construction are humming, copper rises. Gold is the opposite kind of metal: it does nothing useful in an economy, people buy it when they are worried. Divide one by the other and you get a rough gauge of optimism about global industry, with China doing most of the work. A rising ratio says factories are busy and investors are calm. A falling ratio says demand is fading or fear is rising, or both.

[[fig:1]]

The top panel shows the copper to gold ratio, the bottom panel shows the Nifty Metal index over the same period. Notice how the two tend to turn together: the long slide into 2016, the sharp rebound after the pandemic as Chinese stimulus and global restocking kicked in, and the flatter, choppier years after the property bust. The marker for the yuan devaluation of 2015 sits near a low point in both. That is the point: Indian steel, aluminium, zinc and mining stocks are priced off the same global cycle that copper tracks, and that cycle runs through Chinese demand.

Two cautions. Copper can rise for reasons unrelated to China, such as mine disruptions or the rush to build power grids and data centres, and gold has its own drivers, including central banks buying it to diversify away from the dollar. Read the ratio as a weather vane, not a thermometer.

The vane swings hardest on Chinese stimulus. Since the property bust Beijing has preferred measured doses, rate cuts and easier rules for home buyers, and each headline tends to spark a rally in metal stocks worldwide, India included, that fades when the details look small. A real turn needs three things together: credit to households and private firms accelerating, producer prices turning positive, and home prices ending their slide. Until then, assume China keeps exporting its excess.

sections.heading: China plus one: the orders India wins, and the value it does not keep
sections.html:
The phrase China plus one became popular after 2018, when the first round of US tariffs on Chinese goods made multinationals realise that having every factory in one country was a risk, not just a cost saving. The pandemic made the point unforgettable. Companies did not leave China. They added a second base. India, Vietnam, Mexico and Indonesia competed to be that second base.

India's pitch was a huge home market, cheap engineering talent, and from 2020, the production linked incentive schemes, which pay manufacturers a cash reward for every extra unit they make in India. Smartphones became the poster child. Apple's contract manufacturers, Taiwanese firms such as Foxconn and later an Indian conglomerate, scaled up assembly so fast that phones became one of India's largest exports.

But look one layer down. A phone assembled in Chennai is full of displays, camera modules, batteries, circuit boards and chips, and a large share of those still arrive from China. The same is true of solar modules made from Chinese cells and wafers, and of medicines. India's pharma industry, the pharmacy of the world, imports a big share of the active ingredients and the chemical starting materials behind them from China. That was not always so. In the 1990s, cheap Chinese supplies made Indian penicillin plants unviable and they shut. Only in the last few years, with incentive money, have new plants started making some of those molecules again.

India is winning the last step of the factory line faster than the steps behind it.

There is a policy knot here. After the border clash of 2020, India required government approval for any investment from countries that share a land border, which in practice meant China. That kept Chinese money out of sensitive sectors, but it also made it harder for Chinese component makers to build plants in India, which is exactly what deeper supply chains would need. In March 2026 the cabinet eased the rule for small investments. Watch how far that easing goes. It is the clearest sign of whether India wants Chinese capital as a partner in China plus one, or only Chinese customers' orders.

sections.heading: Rare earths: the choke point China showed it would use
sections.html:
Rare earths are a group of metals with names nobody remembers, neodymium, dysprosium, terbium and friends, that make extraordinarily strong magnets. Those magnets sit in electric vehicle motors, wind turbines, missiles, hard drives, phone speakers and the small motors that move a car's seats and windows. China mines most of the world's rare earths and does an even larger share of the refining and magnet-making, because for decades it was willing to accept the pollution and the thin margins that everyone else walked away from.

For years that dominance was an economic fact. Then it became a policy tool. In July 2023 China announced licence requirements on exports of gallium and germanium, two metals used in chips, widely read as a reply to American controls on chip technology. In April 2025, in the middle of the tariff war with the United States, it put rare-earth magnets under a licensing regime that demanded detailed end-use documents. Exporters needed permission, and permission was slow.

India was collateral damage. Indian carmakers and two-wheeler makers, especially those building electric models, warned the government of possible production halts. Then in October 2025 Beijing announced a much wider package covering rare-earth technology, battery materials and more. After Donald Trump and Xi Jinping met in Busan at the end of that month, China agreed to suspend the October package for a year. The April licensing stayed in place.

Here is why this matters for valuations. A dependency that is merely cheap gets priced as a cost. A dependency that can be switched off gets priced as a risk. Indian EV makers, electronics assemblers and defence suppliers now carry a supply-chain risk premium that did not exist a few years ago, and the suspension's one-year clock means the question returns in late 2026. The response, from India and others, is to look for new mines, recycling and magnet plants outside China. Those take years, so the lever stays in Beijing's hand for now.

history_title: six times China moved Indian markets

history.title: The factory of the world opens for business
history.story:
China spent the better part of fifteen years negotiating to join the World Trade Organization, with Premier Zhu Rongji pushing reforms at home and trade negotiator Long Yongtu grinding through talks abroad. In December 2001 it finally became a member.

What followed was the most extraordinary export boom in history. Multinationals moved production to the Pearl River Delta by the thousand, and Chinese scale reset the world price of almost anything that could be made on an assembly line. Indian manufacturers in labour-intensive goods found themselves competing against factories many times their size, with better ports and cheaper power.
history.lesson: Since 2001 the relevant competitor for most Indian manufacturing has not been the company down the road; it has been China's marginal factory.

history.title: The Sunday that lit the commodity fire
history.story:
In November 2008, with Lehman Brothers freshly bankrupt and world trade collapsing, China's State Council announced on a Sunday a stimulus programme worth almost a fifth of the country's economy, to be spent over about two years on railways, roads, power grids and housing. Premier Wen Jiabao's government also told banks to lend, and they did, in quantities nobody had seen before.

Shanghai stocks surged the next day, and metal stocks around the world followed. The building spree that followed pulled iron ore, copper and coal into a supercycle that ran into 2011. For Indian metal and mining companies, many of which had borrowed heavily to buy assets abroad just before the crisis, it was a lifeline.
history.lesson: Chinese credit is the commodity cycle. When Beijing really opens the tap, Indian metal stocks move before the steel is even poured.

history.title: The devaluation nobody saw coming
history.story:
The summer of 2015 had already been brutal for Chinese investors: a margin-fuelled stock bubble had burst, and the government had ordered state funds to buy shares to stop the fall. Then, in August, the People's Bank of China under Zhou Xiaochuan cut the yuan's value overnight, its biggest one-day move in two decades, and changed how the daily rate was set.

Markets read it as a sign that China's economy was weaker than its numbers said, and that it might export its problems through a cheaper currency. Two weeks later came a day traders called Black Monday: Shanghai collapsed, and in Mumbai the Sensex suffered what was then the biggest single-day wipeout of investor wealth in Indian market history. Metal stocks were hit hardest.
history.lesson: A China growth scare reaches India through two pipes at once: foreign funds selling emerging markets, and metal prices falling.

history.title: Galwan, and the door that closed
history.story:
In the panic of early 2020, as Indian shares crashed with the pandemic, filings showed that the People's Bank of China had lifted its stake in HDFC, the mortgage lender, to just above the level that requires disclosure. It was a small holding, but it caused a furore. Within days India announced that investment from any country sharing a land border would need government approval, explicitly to stop opportunistic takeovers.

Then, one night in June, Indian and Chinese soldiers fought hand to hand in the Galwan valley in Ladakh, without firearms, and twenty Indian soldiers were killed. India banned dozens of Chinese apps, including TikTok, at the end of the month, and Chinese firms found government contracts harder to win. Trade, oddly, kept growing, because Indian factories still needed Chinese parts.
history.lesson: Geopolitics sets the limits of economic integration, but it rarely cuts the supply chain itself, and markets price that difference.

history.title: Evergrande and the long deflation
history.story:
Hui Ka Yan built Evergrande into the most indebted property developer in the world, with projects in hundreds of cities and a football club on the side. When the three red lines cut off new bank loans, the model collapsed. Evergrande began missing payments in September 2021, angry homebuyers and investors protested outside its offices, and in January 2024 a Hong Kong court ordered it liquidated. Its shares were finally delisted in 2025.

The slow-motion collapse of Chinese property took construction demand with it. Steel mills that had fed the apartment boom turned to export markets, and Indian steelmakers watched Chinese offers undercut them. That is what pushed Indian mills to lobby for the safeguard duty of 2025.
history.lesson: Chinese deflation is India's import price ceiling. When China's builders stop, its mills start shipping.

history.title: The magnet squeeze
history.story:
In April 2025, in the thick of its tariff battle with Washington, China put rare-earth magnets under a licence regime. Shipments to India stalled at Chinese ports. By late May, Bajaj Auto was warning of a dark cloud over supply and Maruti Suzuki had scaled back early production plans for its first electric car. Industry bodies lobbied Delhi to intervene.

In October Beijing announced even broader controls. Then, after Donald Trump and Xi Jinping met in Busan at the end of the month, China suspended the new package for a year, while keeping the April rules. Trump declared the rare-earth issue settled. Analysts noted that China still held the cards.
history.lesson: Supply-chain dependence is a lever China is willing to pull, and a one-year pause is a deadline, not a resolution.

today:
The copper to gold ratio in the chart above is the quickest read on whether markets think Chinese and global factory demand is firming or fading, and the Nifty Metal panel shows how closely Indian metal stocks are tracking it right now. Oil at [[val:brent]] a barrel adds a twist: it raises costs for factories everywhere, China's included, so a falling copper to gold ratio in this environment can mean demand destruction rather than Chinese weakness alone.

On policy, India in October 2026 joined the United States and other large economies in a joint statement on structural excess capacity in manufacturing, without naming China and without announcing tariffs; technical talks are due by December. Watch three things next: whether Beijing extends the rare-earth suspension before its one-year clock runs out in late 2026, whether China's producer prices stop falling, and how far India goes in easing the approval rule on Chinese investment.
sowhat:
China sets the price for some Indian sectors and sets the supply for others. Know which one you own.

  • Metals and commodity chemicals live under the Chinese price ceiling. They do best when Chinese stimulus is real or duties are in place, and worst when Chinese producer prices are falling.
  • Prefer users over producers when Chinese deflation is deep: infrastructure builders, solar developers, appliance and auto makers that buy steel, chemicals and components cheaply.
  • Be careful with companies whose profits depend on a single anti-dumping or safeguard duty. Duties expire, get diluted, or get offset by imports rerouted through third countries.
  • Electronics, EVs and pharma win orders from China plus one, but carry a supply risk on Chinese components, active ingredients and rare-earth magnets. Firms building their own component or ingredient capacity deserve a closer look than pure assemblers.
  • Defence and EV suppliers should be judged partly on how exposed they are to magnet supply.

What would flip it: a large Chinese stimulus that turns its producer prices positive would lift the ceiling over Indian metals and chemicals. A renewed rare-earth or critical-minerals squeeze, on the other hand, would hit the China plus one winners hardest.
